about: What "always allow" remembers from a Bash command a person approved — one set of cases both
clients are proved against. `bashRules.spec.ts` walks it through `bashCommandRules`, which the web
card calls; OrbitKit's `ApprovalRememberParityTests` walks the same file through
`Approvals.bashCommandRules` on Linux. A rule change starts here and lands at both ends or neither.
Each case: `command` (the approval's `input.command`, exactly as the engine sent it) and `rules` —
the command prefixes remembered, in order, each stored as `Bash(<prefix>:*)`. An empty list means
the card offers no remember action at all.

cases.name: a blank command remembers nothing
whitespace alone remembers nothing
one command: the program and its sub-command
a flag ends the prefix
env assignments ahead of the program are skipped
a subshell has no clean program word
Codex's shell wrapper is never remembered
the card from 2026-10-02: Codex's multi-line /bin/bash -lc script
cases.command:
/bin/bash -lc "set -o pipefail
printf '%s\\n' '--- recent errors ---'
docker compose logs --no-color --since=5m apiserver 2>&1 | grep -E 'ERROR|P2020|approval|approval|ExceptionsHandler' | tail -120 || true
printf '%s\\n' '--- recent warnings ---'
docker compose logs --no-color --since=5m apiserver 2>&1 | grep -E 'WARN|BadEnvironmentKey' | tail -40 || true"

cases.name: a wrapper anywhere in a compound line refuses the whole line
a wrapper behind a pipe
a wrapper behind an env assignment
a wrapper spelled --command
a wrapper named inside quotes is only text
a sub-command that recurs is remembered once
cases.command: git add a; git status; git add b

cases.name: a bareword second word keeps the rule narrow
quoted arguments fall back to the program
every sub-command of a compound line, not just the leading cd
cases.command: cd /root/.orbit/worktrees/019f04fc; git add -A src/macos; echo "=== any isSystem refs left anywhere? ==="; grep -rn "isSystem" src/macos || echo "(none — good)"; echo "=== any conflict markers left? ==="; grep -rn "^<<<<<<<\|^=======\|^>>>>>>>" src/macos || echo "(none — good)"; echo "=== unmerged files? ==="; git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U || true; echo "(empty = all resolved)"

cases.name: a quoted separator does not split a sub-command
a backslash-escaped pipe inside quotes stays one sub-command
newlines separate sub-commands
a backslash inside single quotes closes nothing early and hides nothing after it
an ordinary backslash inside single quotes stays one sub-command
a quote inside single quotes, the shell's own way, stays one sub-command
ANSI-C quoting, where a backslash does escape
a comment ends at its newline, and what follows is a sub-command
an apostrophe in a comment opens no quote
cases.command:
git add -A # don't push
git status

cases.name: a separator in a comment splits nothing
a line that is only a comment remembers nothing
a # inside a word is not a comment
a quoted # is not a comment
a line continuation does not start a word
a comment after a line continuation is still a comment
a shell keyword alone is never remembered: it names no program
cases.command:
for f in a b
do
  ./run.sh
done

cases.name: a keyword ahead of something that is no clean word is never remembered either
a keyword ahead of a program word names that program
cases.command: for f in a; do echo x; done

cases.name: a single-quoted heredoc's body is not a sub-command
cases.command:
cat > notes.txt <<'EOF'
git status
npm test
EOF

cases.name: an unquoted heredoc's body is not a sub-command
cases.command:
cat > notes.txt <<EOF
git status
npm test
EOF

cases.name: a double-quoted delimiter
a backslash-quoted delimiter
a partly quoted delimiter is the word with its quotes removed
a quoted delimiter can hold a space
cases.command:
cat <<'END OF'
git status
END OF
ls

cases.name: a space between the operator and its word
cases.command:
cat << EOF
git status
EOF
ls

cases.name: no space ahead of the operator
a file descriptor ahead of the operator
what follows the terminator is a sub-command again
cases.command:
cat <<'EOF'
npm test
EOF
git status

cases.name: <<- lets tabs indent the terminator
<<- with its word set apart
<<- takes tabs off the terminator, not spaces
cases.command:
cat <<-EOF
  EOF
git status
	EOF
ls

cases.name: plain << lets nothing indent the terminator
cases.command:
cat <<EOF
	EOF
git status
EOF
ls

cases.name: more than one heredoc on a line: their bodies follow in order
cases.command:
cat <<ONE <<TWO
git status
ONE
npm test
TWO
ls

cases.name: heredocs of two sub-commands on one line
cases.command:
cat <<ONE; wc -l <<TWO
git status
ONE
npm test
TWO
ls

cases.name: a second terminator is only body until the first body has ended
cases.command:
cat <<ONE <<TWO
TWO
ONE
git status
TWO
ls

cases.name: one heredoc after another
cases.command:
cat <<ONE
git status
ONE
wc -l <<TWO
npm test
TWO
ls

cases.name: a heredoc into a pipe
cases.command:
cat <<EOF | grep -v x
git status
EOF
ls

cases.name: a sub-command behind the word stays on its line
a separator right behind the word
a comment behind the word
cases.command:
cat <<EOF # note
git status
EOF
ls

cases.name: a # inside the word is part of it
a line continuation does not start the body
a quoted newline does not start the body
cases.command:
cat <<EOF "a
b"
git status
EOF
ls

cases.name: an apostrophe in a body opens no quote
cases.command:
cat <<'EOF'
it's here
EOF
git status

cases.name: a double quote in an unquoted heredoc's body opens no quote
a separator in a body splits nothing
cases.command:
cat <<'EOF'
notes; git status && npm test
EOF

cases.name: a shell wrapper in a body is only text
a terminator is a whole line and nothing else
cases.command:
cat <<EOF
EOF 
 EOF
EOF x
xEOF
git status
EOF
ls

cases.name: a terminator is compared exactly, not by what it looks like
cases.command:
cat <<'é'
é
git status
é
ls

cases.name: a body with no terminator runs to the end of the command
an empty body is only its terminator
a backslash-newline joins two body lines, so the second cannot terminate
cases.command:
cat <<EOF
git status\
EOF
npm test
EOF
ls

cases.name: an escaped backslash at the end of a body line joins nothing
nothing past a terminator a backslash joins is read: shells differ on it
cases.command:
cat <<EOF
EOF\

git status
EOF
ls

cases.name: the same when <<- takes the tabs off what a backslash joined
cases.command:
cat <<-EOF
\
		EOF
git status
EOF
ls

cases.name: under a quoted delimiter a backslash joins nothing
a backslash in the delimiter quotes it too
a heredoc inside an unquoted substitution
a heredoc inside a double-quoted substitution stays one argument
cases.command:
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
fix one thing

git status
EOF
)"

cases.name: a here-string is not a heredoc: the next line is a sub-command
a # right behind a here-string's operator starts a comment
a quoted here-string is not a heredoc either
a here-string beside a heredoc
ordinary lines around a single < stay sub-commands
a quoted << is only text
an escaped < starts no heredoc
a << in a comment is only a comment
a shift inside $(( )) is not a heredoc
a << inside a bare (( counts as a heredoc: a plain sh has no such arithmetic
a parenthesis inside an arithmetic does not close it
a quoted (( hides no heredoc
a $(( that turns out to be two subshells hides no heredoc after it
cases.command:
echo $((ls) && (pwd) )
cat <<EOF
git status
EOF
ls

cases.name: an arithmetic that has closed hides no heredoc
an operator with no word on its line is no heredoc
an operator with a separator for a word is no heredoc
a command that stops at the operator
a command that stops at <<-
a command that stops at the word
a command that stops at the newline after the word
a command that stops at a backslash in the word
a command that stops at a backslash in a body
an open quote in the word runs to the end of the command
